name: FDS Institut
platform: Web app · public site · learner portal
role: Head of Digital Transformation — sole designer & developer
lead: The public site and the whole operating system of a Goethe-certified language centre: enrolment, billing, attendance, scheduling, certificates and online exams — plus myFDS, the learners' own space.
problem: The institute ran on Excel and paper. Receipts were written by hand, certificates took a long time to produce, printed tests were slow to grade, and learners could only pay or ask anything by coming in person. Every exam session meant closing the doors.
hmw: How might we give the office, the teachers and the learners one shared system — without anyone seeing data that isn't theirs?
research: Interviews with the director and office staff
Audit of paper forms and Excel files
findings: Every receipt, list and certificate was retyped by hand, so the office was always behind.
Printed tests and manual grading forced the institute to pause classes.
No way to check a schedule, a payment or a document without coming in.
users: I want to enrol, bill and print in one place.
Retyping the same learner in three files.
I want my groups and attendance on my phone.
I want to see my classes, payments and certificates.
Has to come in for every question.
mood: Warm cream, deep navy and a single orange for action — serious enough for an exam centre, warm enough for a school.

fonts.dNote: custom brand face — previewed here with a close substitute
fonts.bNote: custom brand face — previewed here with a close substitute

solutionNote: The public site, the staff back office and the learner portal share one database. Row Level Security in PostgreSQL decides who sees what.
outcome: Receipts, lists and certificates now come out of the platform.
Tests are taken and graded online.
Schedule, payments and documents are one login away.

name: GoodLoc' Permis
lead: An SAAQ-approved driving school in Montreal with two branches — courses from first licence to refresher training, a path for newcomers, and online registration.
problem: People arrive with very different needs: a first licence, getting back behind the wheel, or exchanging a foreign licence after moving to Quebec. The offer was hard to compare and most sign-ups still went through the phone.
hmw: How might we route every visitor to the right course and get them registered without a phone call?
findings: Beginners, refreshers and newcomers all landed on the same page.
Licence exchange rules are confusing and need their own explanation.
Questions about the SAAQ exam are how many learners find a school.
users: I want to know what the class 5 course includes.
I want to exchange my licence quickly.
I want registrations to arrive complete.
mood: Bold orange with friendly round type — energetic, reassuring and easy to read at a glance.

app.title: My licence
app.sub: Your path to the SAAQ exam
app.caption: Student space — concept

solutionNote: Packages, the newcomer path and the blog all lead to the same registration flow.
outcome: Beginners, refreshers and newcomers each have their route.
Guides and FAQ answer the questions learners type.

name: Elite Partners
lead: Corporate site for a consulting firm that helps companies set up and grow in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
problem: Years of expertise across sectors lived in brochures and conversations. Foreign investors and local companies had no clear place to see what the firm does and how to start working with it.
hmw: How might we make a broad consulting offer readable in a minute, in French and in English?
findings: Services cut across several sectors and needed two entry points.
Local companies read French, foreign investors often English.
Visitors want proof and a person to talk to before anything else.
users: I want to understand the market and who can guide me.
I want help to structure and grow.
I want to see the firm's credibility.
mood: Deep ink and corporate blue with a violet gradient on calls to action — modern, confident, international.

admin.title: Incoming leads
admin.caption: Lead inbox — concept for the contact pipeline

solutionNote: A corporate site where every section ends on the same next step: a first conversation.
outcome: Services and sectors are two clear doors into the same expertise.
French and English from every page.
Each section ends on a call to action.

name: Voilà Vélo
platform: Website with event booking · FR / EN
lead: An event service in Montreal that rents pedal-powered smoothie blenders — for schools, offices, malls and parties.
problem: The offer goes from a single child-sized bike to a full parade. Clients struggled to pick the right package, and every booking turned into a long exchange of emails.
hmw: How might we let an event organiser pick a package and book in one sitting, in their language?
findings: Organisers choose by event type, not by bike model.
Every page should lead to a booking request.
Montreal clients expect both French and English.
users: I want a fun activity that teaches healthy habits.
Unsure which package fits a class.
I want a team activity that's easy to book.
I want something different for a birthday.
mood: Juicy coral, honey and leaf green on cream — playful like the bikes, clean like a food brand.
solutionNote: Every package page ends on the booking form, in French or English.
outcome: Organisers start from their event, not from a catalogue.
Requests arrive with date, place and package.
The whole site switches FR / EN.

name: Ayan Bridge
lead: A learning platform that grew past its course catalogue: lessons, an AI studio, a marketplace and an investment arm under one account.
problem: Four products in one account meant four menus. Learners opened the app and didn't know where they had stopped or what to do next.
hmw: How might we make the dashboard answer one question: what should I do now?
findings: Progress was buried inside each course.
Without visible progress, streaks and rewards, learners drop off.
Studio, Learn Hub and Capital fought for the same space.
users: I want to pick up where I left off.
I want to publish and track my courses.
I want my projects and learning in one place.
mood: Near-black surfaces with gold for rewards and blue for progress — focused like an IDE, rewarding like a game.
solutionNote: A dark dashboard built around the next lesson, with rewards close enough to keep learners coming back.
outcome: The current course and next lesson open the dashboard.
XP, rankings and achievements on the home screen.
Learn Hub, Studio and Capital under one bar.

name: AutoTechno
lead: A catalogue and delivery platform for automotive professionals — ECU files, airbag and dashboard solutions, diagnostic software — with tokens and an admin back office.
problem: Files were sent by hand over messaging apps. Finding the right file for a precise vehicle was slow, payments were tracked manually, and the catalogue lived in folders.
hmw: How might we let a garage find, pay for and download the right file in a few clicks?
research: Interviews with the owner and a tuner
findings: Professionals search by brand, model and ECU — never by product name.
A token wallet fits better than one payment per file.
Uploads, prices and orders must be managed without a developer.
users: I want the right file now, for this car.
Waits for a reply on chat.
I want my past downloads in one place.
I want to add files and follow orders.
mood: Workshop black with amber — technical, high contrast, made for screens in a garage.
solutionNote: Customers buy with tokens and download instantly; the team runs the catalogue from its own back office.
outcome: Brand and model pages lead straight to the files.
Files, orders and posts managed by the team.

name: Tasshila
lead: An e-health platform that reads biological lab results from a photograph of the report, explains each value and follows it over time.
problem: Patients receive lab reports on paper or as PDFs. The values, units and reference ranges are hard to read, and from one test to the next nobody keeps a history.
hmw: How might a patient understand their own results from a simple photo — and see how they change?
research: Literature on OCR for medical documents
findings: Each lab prints names, units and ranges differently.
Patients mostly want to know: is this normal?
Results end up in drawers, not in a timeline.
users: I want to know if my results are fine.
I want to follow my values over time.
I want a clean history at the consultation.
mood: Clinical teal and mint with a warm coral for alerts — calm, trustworthy and readable.
solutionNote: Concept screens for the thesis prototype — to be replaced with screenshots of the real app.
outcome: Names, values, units and ranges extracted from an image.
Each value placed against its reference range.
Reports become a timeline the patient can read.

name: Tiger Bec Cars
lead: Showcase site for a family dealer in Quebec that selects cars of character and sells them one by one.
problem: The dealer's cars were listed like any inventory: a photo, a price, a line of specs. The story behind each car — and the family behind the dealer — was lost.
hmw: How might each car read like a piece with a history, not a line in a stock list?
findings: Clients come for the car's history and the dealer's eye.
The best photos were hidden in small thumbnails.
Buyers want to talk to someone, not fill a long form.
users: I want to know where this car comes from.
I want to browse the collection like a gallery.
I want my cars to look as good online as in the showroom.
mood: Black brick, white type and a red glow — a night-time showroom.
solutionNote: A dark, quiet design where large photography and the family story carry the sale.
outcome: Each vehicle gets its own space and story.
The family history is part of the experience.
Contact is one tap away from every car.

name: Picci
lead: A family business serving drivers since the eighties — car wash, mechanics, barbershop, car sales and financing under one roof.
problem: Four unrelated trades shared one address. Online, each looked like a different business, and clients didn't know the station offered more than a wash.
hmw: How might four different services read as one coherent station — without any of them getting lost?
findings: Clients come for one service and leave not knowing the others exist.
The family history and the building are recognised in the area.
Most clients phone or drive by rather than book online.
users: I want my car washed and checked in one stop.
I want a used car and financing together.
I want my haircut while the car is washed.
mood: Night photography of the building with red accents and a classic serif — local, proud and a little vintage.

fonts.dNote: display serif — previewed with a close substitute

solutionNote: One identity and one card per trade, each leading to a call or directions.
outcome: Four trades read as one place.
Every service has its own page.
Call and directions on every page.

name: Queen de Q
lead: Pre-launch site for a playful self-discovery app: draw a card, discover an archetype, join the waiting list and unlock perks at launch.
problem: A personal-development app with humour can't look like a corporate landing page. The brand needed a first visit that felt like a game — and still filled a waiting list.
hmw: How might the first visit feel like opening a gift, and end with a sign-up?
findings: A small game invites people further than a promise.
Limited places make joining feel special.
Humour and warmth must carry every line.
users: I want to know what this is about.
I want early access and perks.
No reason to sign up early.
I want to meet women like me.
No place to gather before launch.
mood: Plum night, gold script and soft rose — a royal, playful world with a wink.

fonts.dNote: script — previewed with a close substitute

solutionNote: An illustrated, deliberately unusual interface where every interaction leads to the waiting list.
outcome: The card draw invites people in.
Limited places shown live make joining feel special.

name: BDTECH
lead: Site for an IT services company that selects, integrates and deploys equipment for businesses — infrastructure, security and mobility.
problem: Decision-makers landing on the company had to dig to understand its scope. Services, partners and contact were spread across documents and calls.
hmw: How might a busy decision-maker understand the scope and ask for a quote in one visit?
findings: Visitors want to know if the company covers their need before reading more.
Clients prefer to talk to someone quickly.
users: I want a partner for workstations and network security.
I want to know if they're credible.
I want access to my documents and support.
mood: Navy and electric blue on white with floating hardware — clean, technical and corporate.
solutionNote: A clear corporate site with a client login behind it.
outcome: Infrastructure, security and mobility in the first screen.
Story, vision and partners build trust.
Call and email from every section.

name: GoodPc
lead: A refurbished-technology retailer in Canada — a marketplace built to make second-hand hardware feel like a premium purchase.
problem: Refurbished hardware carries doubt: is it reliable, is it guaranteed, who checked it? The store had to remove that doubt before the cart.
hmw: How might buying a refurbished laptop feel as safe as buying a new one?
findings: Buyers hesitate without warranty and inspection details.
Clear condition grades make comparison easy.
Many visitors want their own device refurbished.
users: I want a reliable laptop on a budget.
Fear of a bad second-hand buy.
I want several machines with warranty.
mood: Bright white with a blue-to-green gradient — fresh, optimistic and a little techy.
solutionNote: Warranty, grades and support sit next to every product to remove doubt before checkout.
outcome: Warranty, delivery and support shown with products.
Condition is clear at a glance.

name: CFAQ
client: Centre de Formation Aquatique du Québec
lead: An aquatic training centre in Quebec — swimming, lifesaving and water fitness programmes for every age, with a shop and video lessons.
problem: Programmes for toddlers, children, teens and instructors were listed together. Parents and trainees had trouble finding their level, and material was sold separately.
hmw: How might every family or trainee find the right programme in a few taps?
findings: Parents look for their child's age first.
Instructor training is a different audience.
The shop and videos support the courses.
users: I want the right class for my child's age.
Programme names don't say the age.
I want to become a lifeguard.
I want training material and videos.
mood: Pool teal and sunny yellow on white — calm water with a playful touch.
solutionNote: Programmes organised by age, with sign-up, shop and videos in the same account.
outcome: Material and lessons support each programme.

name: Divan Hane
lead: A restaurant site built around appetite: full-bleed food photography, an ornamental identity and a menu that reads as an invitation.
problem: The menu lived as a long price list in a PDF. Nothing online showed the room, the dishes or the warmth of the place.
hmw: How might a menu make people want to come, not just compare prices?
findings: Photos decide the visit more than descriptions.
Most visitors open the site on the street or at the table.
Guests prefer to phone the restaurant.
users: I want to see if it looks good.
I want to know the dishes before coming.
mood: Black, antique gold and wine red with an engraved serif — warm, ornamental, evening light.
solutionNote: Full-bleed photography and a dark ornamental frame, designed for the phone.
outcome: Dishes shown big before any price.
Gold, ornaments and serif type across the site.
The call button follows the visitor.

name: Point de Location
lead: A car rental agency in Annaba that ran on a Word contract template. I built its online presence and fleet catalogue.
problem: Clients couldn't see the fleet, the conditions or what a car included before calling. Every booking started from zero on the phone.
hmw: How might a client choose a car and send a booking request before the first call?
findings: They want specs and conditions side by side.
Deposit and rules were explained again and again.
users: I want a car ready when I land.
No way to see the fleet.
mood: Black and gold from the agency's logo on white — classic and premium.
solutionNote: Each car has its own sheet with a request form; conditions are published once, in two languages.
outcome: Every car with its full spec sheet.
Clients send a request from the car's page.
Conditions clear in French and English.

name: Mobile apps
lead: Three apps shipped with React Native and a Node.js back end: Wassalni for carpooling, Clinical for medical follow-up, Astrolabs for mental health and personal assistance.
problem: Everyday needs — getting a ride, getting care, getting support — still went through phone calls and word of mouth. People needed simple apps on the phone they already carry.
hmw: How might one small team ship three simple apps on one stack?
research: Review of carpooling and health apps
findings: Riders want to know who the driver is before booking.
Users drop apps with long sign-ups.
Rides, appointments and chats share the same building blocks.
users: I want a cheap ride home at the weekend.
I want to share costs on my route.
I want to reach my clinic easily.
mood: Each app has its own colour — blue for Wassalni, green for Clinical, indigo for Astrolabs — on a shared, simple component set.
solutionNote: Presentation boards of the three apps, and the Wassalni flows redrawn.
outcome: Wassalni was selected under the university startup framework.
Astrolabs is live on Google Play.
React Native and Node.js shared across the three apps.
